content: Culturally appropriate spiritual support should be provided to patients and their families upon request. Bereavement support must also be made accessible, which may include bereavement support groups led by adequately trained personnel. Some interventions can be safely and effectively delivered by community health workers (CHWs) with basic training. The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes that the lack of access to palliative care is a significant public health issue. Palliative care should be tailored to the needs of local communities and cultures and integrated into public health systems. This strategy includes fostering political support, analyzing palliative care needs and services, forming a national steering committee, creating an action plan, revising or developing policies on palliative care and pain relief, ensuring access to essential palliative medicines (such as oral fast-acting morphine), initiating training for clinicians, implementing palliative care services at all levels of healthcare, and measuring patient outcomes like quality of life to maintain high standards of care. Community engagement in palliative care delivery is also recommended. Although there are modest start-up costs for implementing this strategy, such as funding for situation analysis, policy development, and training programs, evidence suggests that well-integrated palliative care, including home care, can reduce healthcare costs by decreasing hospital admissions near the end of life. Over time, integrating palliative care into public health systems may become cost-neutral or even save money. However, this strategy assumes a functional primary healthcare (PHC) system. While some lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) like Brazil and Costa Rica have exemplary PHC systems, others, such as Rwanda, are working toward universal access. In many LMICs, PHC systems remain underdeveloped, but palliative care and PHC can be developed and expanded simultaneously. The same infrastructure and human resources used for PHC can also provide basic palliative care, and community-based palliative care efforts can strengthen PHC systems. The shared principles of PHC and palliative care have enabled successful collaborative implementation in places like Kerala, India. The inclusion of palliative care in national healthcare policies is crucial. Without such policies, widespread access and sustainability of palliative care are unlikely. Initial steps toward integration include creating a national palliative care policy mandating access for all, developing a strategic plan with a defined timeline, and incorporating palliative care into national policies on cancer, non-communicable diseases (NCDs), geriatrics, pediatrics, HIV/AIDS, drug-resistant tuberculosis, or PHC. Once these policies are in place, efforts can focus on ensuring the availability of essential medicines (e.g., oral and injectable morphine) and training healthcare providers. Training should begin at a basic level for primary care physicians and those frequently treating patients with serious or life-threatening conditions. Physicians completing basic palliative care training should be authorized to prescribe oral and injectable morphine for both inpatients and outpatients. Intermediate-level training should follow for specialists, practicing nurses, and undergraduate medical, nursing, and pharmacy students. Palliative care services should be integrated into existing healthcare delivery systems at any level, starting where the need is most apparent, such as cancer centers. Initial services may include inpatient wards, consultation services, or outpatient clinics. National policies should mandate palliative care services at all cancer centers and, over time, at all levels of the healthcare system, including secondary and tertiary hospitals, district hospitals, community health centers (CHCs), and home care. Palliative care interventions should be available at each level of the healthcare system. CHWs can provide daily surveillance and emotional support, while nurses, doctors, social workers, or trained lay counselors can offer outpatient care and home visits as needed. Inpatient hospice care may be necessary if families cannot provide adequate care at home. Small palliative care teams, consisting of part-time doctors and nurses with basic or intermediate training, can manage outpatient clinics and inpatient care. Ideally, a palliative care specialist physician should lead teams at major cancer centers and general hospitals. PHC practitioners staffing CHCs and district hospitals should receive basic palliative care training to incorporate it into their standard responsibilities. At least one team leader at district hospitals should have intermediate-level training to serve as a resource for clinicians at CHCs. Palliative care services should be designed based on local needs and values, accessible to patients in their preferred settings (including at home), and comprehensive in addressing physical, psychological, social, and spiritual suffering. These services should be coordinated with other PHC tasks, such as health promotion, disease prevention, and rehabilitative treatment, and provided by clinicians familiar with the patient and family throughout the course of illness. In post-conflict settings, mental health care needs may be particularly significant. Palliative care should ideally be part of a seamless system of illness prevention, early detection, treatment, and rehabilitation. Primary care clinicians play a critical role in recognizing palliative care needs, including uncontrolled symptoms, social distress, and end-of-life care. Early identification of palliative care needs depends on clinicians' knowledge, skills, communication styles, and collaboration with other healthcare providers. Tools are available to assist in identifying these needs, enabling appropriate assessment and intervention. To avoid overburdening already strained primary care clinicians, adequate funding is necessary to employ sufficient staff and strengthen PHC systems. Evidence shows that palliative care services, including home care, can reduce healthcare costs, providing medical, ethical, and financial justification for integrating palliative care into PHC. However, sending patients home for palliative care may place significant physical, mental, and financial strain on family caregivers. Alternatively, terminally ill patients with well-controlled symptoms but inadequate family support could receive end-of-life care at CHCs staffed around the clock, allowing families to visit without the burden of providing 24-hour care. Community participation is a key component of PHC, as identified in the Declaration of Alma-Ata. Communities possess untapped resources and energy that can be mobilized for healthcare delivery. Existing CHWs, who live within the community, can be trained to provide emotional support, monitor symptoms, and report observations to supervising nurses. Nurses can then provide instructions, make home visits, or consult with primary care physicians for further advice. Where CHWs do not exist, community palliative care volunteer networks can be established. Volunteers can receive basic training in palliative care principles and assist primary care teams in providing and monitoring care. Training in palliative care should include pain and symptom management, prognostication, communication skills, and psychosocial and spiritual support. The European Association for Palliative Care (EAPC) undergraduate curriculum identifies these areas as essential competencies. Grassroots palliative care teams should also have basic organizational and coordination skills. The capacity to prevent and relieve suffering and improve quality of life depends on the number, knowledge, skills, and commitment of professional and non-professional caregivers. Core competencies for PHC providers include early identification of suffering, assessment of palliative needs, management of common distressing symptoms, appropriate referrals, and culturally sensitive emotional support and care planning. WHO recommends training requirements for PHC staff providing palliative care, including basic and intermediate-level courses for doctors, nurses, and community-based care team leaders. Medical and nursing students should receive a 30–40-hour basic palliative care course during their final year of training. Continuing education in palliative care should be available to practicing clinicians, with incentives to complete training by a set deadline. Task shifting, as recommended by WHO, allows different members of PHC teams to provide specific palliative care services. Regular supervision is essential to maintain high-quality care. Examples of successful integration of palliative care into PHC include Thailand's nurse-led home care teams and Kerala, India's community-based approach supported by government policies and volunteer networks. However, challenges remain in some settings, such as Uganda, where palliative care is not yet fully integrated into public health systems due to inadequate infrastructure, staff shortages, and unstable funding.
